## 1. FreeToken

[FreeToken](https://github.com/FlashML-org/FreeToken) is FlashML's engine for running mixture-of-experts models. It serves models larger than VRAM by keeping the experts in pinned RAM and caching the hot ones in VRAM.

This does not work for my node with 24GB VRAM + 64GB RAM, this post (& [fork](https://github.com/jomcgi-org/freetoken-fork)) is an experiment where I spill experts to disk to accommodate a larger than memory model.

## 2. Specifications

| Part | Specification |
|---|---|
| Model | Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, 125B parameters, 6B active per token, NVFP4 |
| Expert banks | 63.5 GB, 48 layers of 512 experts |
| Dense layers | 9.2 GB: attention, GDN, embeddings, head |
| Context window | 100k |
| Per-layer embedding (PLE), n-gram lookup table | 27 GB |
| Served in total | about 100 GB |
| GPU | RTX 4090, 24 GB |
| Host | Ryzen 7800X3D, 64 GB DDR5-6000, 1.9 TB NVMe |
| Engine | [freetoken-fork](https://github.com/jomcgi-org/freetoken-fork) |
| Upstream RAM requirement | 128 GB |

These weights don't fit in VRAM or RAM and I can't convince myself to upgrade in this RAM economy so here we are spilling to disk.

The first diagram uses September 1 budgets. Later updates sit beside each experiment.

![Where are the weights?](figures/memory-tiers.svg)

| Key | Part |
|---|---|
| 1 | RTX 4090, 24 GB. Dense layers, the KV cache and the expert slot cache. Everything else gets streamed in as required. |
| 2 | PCIe 4.0 x16. The route for experts to get into VRAM. |
| 3 | Pinned host memory: split between 40 GB of warm expert layers and 6 GB of hot rows. |
| 4 | Page cache, about 16 GB. Kernel-managed cache that reduces the thrashing when accessing disk layers |
| 5 | NVMe, 1.9 TB. All experts banked (63.5 GB) and the 27 GB lookup table |
| 6 | CPU MoE executor, 8 cores, decoding the cold tail out of the page cache |

## 3. Performance

Initially with freetoken this didn't run, start is my first naive attempt at managing experts on disk.

| | Start (tok/s) | End (tok/s) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Prefill | 54 | 346 |
| Single stream | 3.8 | 24 |
| Eight streams, aggregate | 9.6 | 42 |

## 4. How does MoE inference work?

Each token triggers a small number of experts. The location of their weights decides how long it takes to access them and the type of compute they land on.

![MoE Expert selection](figures/moe-selection.svg)

![Expert transfer vs bandwidth](figures/expert-paths.svg)

## 5. Bottlenecks

The many problems I ran into trying to get this working with a reasonably responsive throughput.

### 5.1 Before the request

#### Pinning too much starved the page cache

FreeToken pins expert banks into memory. My initial budget was 52/64 GB, which left nothing for the page cache to manage access to 59.5 GB of disk-resident expert banks.

This was terrible: 96k major faults per decode step and 3.8 tok/s.

Dropping the budget to 40 GB tripled throughput by letting the page cache manage the disk reads.

I now budget pinning and paging together. Growing KV between requests instead of reserving the full 100k context also freed 14% more GPU expert slots at startup. Long conversations take those slots back.

### 5.2 Prefill

#### Prefill was copying whole layers

The upstream implementation streams whole expert layers to the GPU. For a disk-resident layer that meant paging in the entire bank regardless of prompt length.

My patch routed prefill for disk layers through the CPU executor which only touches experts that the router selected.

This reduced the time to process 441 tokens from 17 min to 29 s.

With some layers pinned and some on disk the pinned layers could overlap their PCIe transfer with compute while the disk layers prefilled on the CPU and chained the next pinned layer's prefetch. This took warm prefill from 54 to 116 tok/s.

![Prefill chunk decisions](figures/prefill-chunk.svg)

| Key | Part |
|---|---|
| 1 | Before the forward: the chunk's n-gram ids are computed from its input tokens and deduped. Nothing about them depends on the forward |
| 2 | One read each: the deduped table rows arrive in one coalesced read into a pinned GPU bank; after each layer's routing, its expert rows are populated into the page cache with real reads instead of advisory hints |
| 3 | Forward: the lookup resolves against the pinned bank by compact local id while the experts compute. Major faults per chunk fell from about 3.6 million to a few thousand |
| A | GPU, with the pinned staging bank |
| C | Page cache |
| D | NVMe: lookup table and expert banks |
| E | CPU MoE executor |

Adding the GPU hot set and batching cold routes on CPU brought a new 26,812-token document to its first token in 77.4 seconds on September 3. Similar sizes took 7 to 14 minutes on September 1. This is separate from the short warm benchmark.

One trap here: a prefill benchmark has to miss the prefix cache. Otherwise I can measure how quickly I skipped the work and think I've improved it.

### 5.3 Decode

#### Random reads from disk (experts vs n-gram)

Random reads are fine for experts because on disk they are a read-only mmap of the weight file. Routing happens before the expert computes, so we know what we need to load before it gets used. With some batch deduplication I got under 10 major faults per step for managing them.

The n-gram lookup is different. It's touched on every token at random rows from inside a CUDA graph. Having the GPU read the host file mappings directly was faster than trying to manage this in the caching tiers. Switching to that almost doubled four-stream throughput from 14 to 26.5, and freed the pinned cache that the table had been using, leaving room to fit more experts onto higher-bandwidth tiers.

That didn't last. Two UVM kernel failures later I switched to `io_uring`: dedupe the known n-gram rows, stage them in pinned memory, then copy to GPU. September 3: 0.47 ms per decode step, zero PLE major faults. Expert-bank faults remained.

Advising already-resident pages cost time too. Skipping `MADV_WILLNEED` for experts used within 256 steps on the same layer cut about 8 ms from a 41 ms step. A fault guard restores conservative advice when needed.

#### CPU tier shifting experts on demand

Residency was decided per layer, either pinned or on disk. But our router didn't spread load evenly across experts. Depending on the task a small number of experts may serve most of the routes while the rest are used occasionally.

Pinning the hot rows (about 6 GB covering 72% of routes) and sending them through the GPU's expert slot cache while keeping the cold tail on CPU decode took single-stream from 19.5 to 23.1 and eight streams from 34 to 42.2 at peak, which settles to the 21 and 37 in section 3 on mixed traffic.

Distinct experts hitting the CPU per step fell from 58 to 18.

![One decode step through one expert layer](figures/decode-step.svg)

| Key | Part |
|---|---|
| 1 | Route: the router picks this token's experts from 512 in the layer. The n-gram ids are already known from the last few tokens |
| 2 | Sort by residency: each chosen expert is hot (resident on the GPU), pinned (in host memory), or cold (on the NVMe, possibly in the page cache). About 58 distinct experts a step reached the CPU before the hot set, 18 after |
| 3 | Move: pinned experts stream over PCIe into a GPU slot; cold experts are computed by the CPU out of the page cache, with recent-use checks avoiding redundant willneed advice. The n-gram rows are gathered into pinned staging and copied to the GPU before the forward |
| 4 | Compute and tally: the GPU and CPU partial outputs sum, and every routed expert bumps a decayed counter |
| A | RTX 4090: expert slot cache with the hot set resident, KV cache |
| B | Pinned host memory, 40 GB of expert banks |
| C | Page cache |
| D | NVMe: expert banks 63.5 GB, lookup table 27 GB |
| E | CPU MoE executor |

The CPU returns a small activation vector instead of megabytes of weights. Changing worker counts or barrier spinning didn't reliably help once I accounted for page-cache warming.

#### Is it hot or not? Drifting expectations

This was a step in the right direction, but I hardcoded a captured routing profile. As soon as traffic changed the hit rate fell to 62%, wiping out the gain.

I got this back by replacing the static profile with a decayed per-expert counter and bounded background swaps (retire, copy, flip). This recovered the perf lost on generic workloads and improved cold start as the hot set assembled itself.

![How one hot-set slot changes hands without a stall](figures/hot-set-swap.svg)

| Key | Part |
|---|---|
| 1 | Tick: every 1,000 steps the counters are re-ranked. We use that to swap up to 190 experts. |
| 2 | Stage: a background thread copies the newly hot rows from the NVMe into staging, at most 0.5 GB a tick. The retiring expert keeps serving from where it was |
| 3 | Flip: at a step boundary the mapping points at the staged row and the retired slot is free. No route ever sees a half-installed row |
| A | GPU slot cache, one hot slot of the 6 GB |
| D | NVMe expert banks |

Then a long document flooded the counters and displaced experts needed by follow-up turns. I split prefill and decode histories and aimed the hot set at the current phase. The hot plan now survives restarts too.

After a 76k-document prefill, position-matched follow-ups improved from 12.5 to 14.6 tok/s; prefill took 664 vs 652 seconds. An earlier version reached 19.2 tok/s but needed 885 seconds to prefill. I kept the version that didn't slow down reading.

Several experiments never let the adapter tick. Quite difficult to measure an improvement that way.

## 6. Ideas that didn't pan out

I thought these should have worked. They measured as losses on this box.

| Idea | Result | Conclusion |
|---|---|---|
| Fetch cold experts over PCIe | 10 vs 19.5 tok/s; slot-cache churn | CPU wins on the 4090 |
| Split cold work between PCIe and CPU | 13.8 vs 19.5 tok/s | Extra transfers lose |
| Userspace pager | 13 faults/step, still slower than kernel hints | Keep for larger banks with enough cache |
| Prefetch before routing | 48% predictable; twice the pages read | Off |
| Speculative decode | 12.6 vs 18.0 tok/s at 72% acceptance | Drafted tokens still pay the CPU cost |


## 7. Trying a larger machine

I also tried GLM 5.3 Flash NVFP4 on a GCE `g4-standard-48`: a 96 GB RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, about 176 GB of reported host RAM, and four local NVMe SSDs in RAID 0. The converted checkpoint is 177 GiB.

| Experiment | Result |
|---|---:|
| Single stream, September 4, pin budget 112 and hot budget 48 | 12.12 tok/s, mean of three runs |
| Same setup with split histories and phase aim | 12.37 tok/s |
| Cold tail on CPU, pin budget 8 and hot budget 60 | 9.80 tok/s |
| Prefill, September 3, settled run with 2k cold prompts | 257 tok/s |
| Four streams, September 3 | 19.3 tok/s aggregate |

The 4090 tuning didn't all carry over. With 29 of 42 layers pinned and 99.8% hot coverage in the disk layers, better hot-set selection barely helped. Pinned layers still transferred an estimated 3.1 GB per token over PCIe. The CPU path lost here.

I got the storage wrong first: a 5,700-IOPS boot disk delivered 0.08 to 0.92 tok/s. Local NVMe recovered 12.1. A 64 GB host-memory cap was unusable too. The RAM and disks matter as much as the card here.

## 8. What does this actually mean?

Should you go out and buy a 4090 or an RTX 6000 to run models this way?
Probably not. Inference over API is so cheap that unless you've already got the hardware it's likely cheaper to just pay for API pricing.

My takeaway is that frontier intelligence at home is closer than ever and that the serving methods and model releases will only become more efficient.
I'm in the process of moving from Canada to the UK at the moment so this will shape the type of node that I buy when I get over there!

If you want to run it yourself, the quickstart for my fork is here: [QUICKSTART.md](https://github.com/jomcgi-org/freetoken-fork/blob/feat/moe-disk-tier/QUICKSTART.md).

The [benchmark notes](https://github.com/jomcgi-org/freetoken-fork/blob/0b7ad70f925c1a998e09d357243f8ea2e6f899af/bench/RESULTS.md) have the individual experiments and their conditions.
